text: Lesson 10 established that a Normal change needs individual assessment before it's authorized. This lesson covers the risk half of that assessment: how the platform decides whether a Normal change is High, Medium, or Low risk — calculated consistently, not guessed by whoever fills out the form.

Many implementations build the risk assessment as a structured questionnaire — variables, the same mechanism Catalog Item lessons used for request forms, or a dedicated Risk Assessment record related to the change. Real questions ask about concrete, checkable facts: does this affect production, does it touch a business-critical Configuration Item, is there a tested backout plan, has it succeeded before.

Those answers feed into a calculated risk value, commonly a risk field on change_request. One approach is a weighted scoring model, where each answer contributes points and thresholds map total points to a band. Another is a rules-based lookup, where a specific combination — production yes, no backout plan — automatically forces High regardless of anything else.

A calculated risk value nobody acts on is worse than no risk field at all — it creates the appearance of governance with no real effect. The principle that makes this worth building is that higher risk should programmatically require more approval stages: Low risk might need manager approval alone, while Medium or High risk should automatically chain on CAB approval too.

A common mistake is building the questionnaire but leaving the risk field manually settable, so someone can mark a change touching the production database as Low just by selecting it. A correctly implemented instance makes the risk field read-only and system-calculated — the only way to change the risk is to change the real facts behind it.

Calculated consistently, and actually acted on downstream — that's what makes risk assessment real rather than decorative. Next up: building the approval workflow that risk value actually feeds into, chaining manager and CAB approval in Flow Designer.
